title: CAN: Make dissector table can.subdissector (CAN ID) accessible for lua scripts
description:
Change the way the decode as dissector table can.subdissector is created.
Creating the dissector table as FT_UINT32 makes it usable in lua scripts.

Before it was created by using register_decode_as_next_proto which creates a
dissector table of type FT_NONE which is not accessible in lua scripts.

notes.body: Isn't this change likely to break any existing usage of CAN that uses Decode As...?

For my understanding it should not break the existing usage. I tried to add a new feature by staying compatible.
Previously available entries in the Decode as list are still available after the change.
![can.subdissector_decode_as](/uploads/4ea7e1de1bc8a16edd65ca482840e5ac/can.subdissector_decode_as.png)
What is it you're trying to do in your Lua script that can't be done if the dissector table is a "payload" dissector table?

I want to register different dissectors fors different can ids. Like:

`local can_id_dissector_table = DissectorTable.get("can.subdissector")`

`can_id_dissector_table:add(291,trivial_proto)`

But it throws an exception in `DissectorTable_add` which says
> "Strange type %d for a DissectorTable"


What exactly is a payload dissector table?

> What exactly is a payload dissector table?

A dissector table used if protocol A packets have a payload that can be dissected as more than one protocol but where protocol A does *not* have a field that could be used to distinguish packets whose payload should be dissected as one protocol from packets whose payload should be dissected as another protocol.

So a payload dissector table may have several "can be used" dissectors, registered with `dissector_add_for_decode_as()` (which is usable from Lua), but has either zero or one "active" entry - it doesn't have a field associated with it, with multiple entries for different values of the field, mapping a field value to a dissector to be used.

If you want to register dissectors for particular CAN IDs, where "CAN ID" is the ID from the "CAN ID and flags" field in the [LINKTYPE_SOCKETCAN header](https://www.tcpdump.org/linktypes/LINKTYPE_CAN_SOCKETCAN.html), then you will have to modify the packet-socketcan.c dissector to *create* a dissector table, named "can.id" (to match the name of that field in the packet-socketcan.dissector), of type FT_UINT32 (it's only 29 bits long, but that means you need FT_UINT32), have the socket can dissector *use* that table, and register in *that* table.

Does that mean that in my current proposal dissectors which has registered via `dissector_add_for_decode_as()` would not be called anymore?


> you will have to modify the packet-socketcan.c dissector to *create* a dissector table, named "can.id"

Honestly, that was my preferred solution. But I thought it would be confusing having more dissector tables for basically the same information. You would need 2 new dissctor tables. You would need one for 11 bit standard ids (`can.id`) and one for 29 bit extended ids (`can.extended_id`) because both ranges overlap and can be used in the same environment.

> Does that mean that in my current proposal dissectors which has registered via `dissector_add_for_decode_as()` would not be called anymore?

If you have the SocketCAN dissector do something such as:

- if `heuristic_first` is false, trying the appropriate CAN ID dissector table, then trying the payload dissector if nothing is found in the CAN ID dissector table, then trying the heuristic dissector table;
- if `heuristic_first` is true, trying the heuristic dissector table, then trying the appropriate CAN ID dissector table if that doesn't find anything, then trying the payload dissector if nothing is found in the CAN ID dissector table;

then anything added to the "eligible for Decode As..." list for the payload dissector table with `dissector_add_for_decode_as()` would still be called if appropriate - i.e., if nothing is registered for a particular CAN ID and, if `heuristic_first` is true, the packet isn't matched by any heuristic.

Anything that's registered in the "can.subdissector" table should also be registered in the new tables, so that the user can force them to be used for a particular CAN ID as well as for "use this if nothing else matches".

If that means that there's no longer a reason to *have* the "can.subdissector" table - i.e., if it's sufficient to allow the user to say "dissect packets with this particular CAN ID as XXX" without also allowing them to say "dissect everything not otherwise matched as XXX" - then you can get rid of the "can.subdissector" table.

> But I thought it would be confusing having more dissector tables for basically the same information. You would need 2 new dissctor tables. You would need one for 11 bit standard ids (`can.id`) and one for 29 bit extended ids (`can.extended_id`) because both ranges overlap and can be used in the same environment.

If "confusing having more dissector tables for basically the same information" you mean "two tables for the CAN ID, one for standard and one for extended", then it may be confusing, but it's also *necessary* if, as you seem to be saying, standard CAN ID 17 and extended CAN ID 17 can be used on the same network, with *different* protocols being transported in standard CAN ID 17 packets and extended CAN ID 17 packets.

In that case, you go with "confusing but works" rather than "not confusing but doesn't work".

And, if you need to have your add-on dissectors work with particular CAN IDs, rather than just being specified as "use this for all packets not matched by any heuristic", you also have no choice about creating dissector tables for CAN IDs.

Thanks for your explanation!

Whats your opinion how to proceed?

**Option A:** Introduce 2 new dissector tables for CAN IDs (`can.id` and `can.extended_id`) and **remove** existing `can.subdissector`. (This would affact other dissectors aswell)

**Option B:** Introduce 2 new dissector tables for CAN IDs (`can.id` and `can.extended_id`) and **keep** existing `can.subdissector` (This would not affact other dissectors and would be a compatible extension)

**Option C:** Do not introduce new dissector tables for CAN IDs and rewrite the change in a way that the functions are called in that order (for heuristic_first == false, for heuristic_first == true -> accordingly):

1. `dissector_try_uint_new()`
2. `dissector_try_payload_new()`
3. `dissector_try_heuristic()`
4. `call_data_dissector()`

**Option D:** Take the change as it is at the moment. (Not sure if I miss something but for my understanding it should do the job without being a breaking change.)

Notes:

- It is possible to diffenrentiate between standard and extended CAN IDS with `can.subdissector` but it is done in a strange way. One of the most significant bits is used to indicate if its an extended id.
- I don't understand the difference between `dissector_try_uint_new()` and `dissector_try_payload_new()` since `dissector_try_payload_new()` is doing nothing but calling `dissector_try_uint_new()` under the hood.

> Whats your opinion how to proceed?

It depends on whether there will ever be a need for a user to say "dissect all CAN messages where no dissector is registered for a given ID and where no heuristic matches the contents as this protocol".

From a quick look at some documents discussing CAN, the answer might be "no"; they seem to indicate that the ID indicates the content of the message in some form, so it's more like an EtherType field than an address.

If that's the case, then I would go with option A, and change dissectors that register themselves in can.subdissector for Decode As to register in can.id and can.extended_id, instead.

Otherwise, I'd go with option B, change dissectors that register themselves in can.subdissector for Decode As to register in can.id and can.extended_id, *in addition*, so that somebody can say "dissect everything unmatched as XXX" *or* "dissect frames with an ID of AAA as XXX" or "dissect frames with an extended ID of BBB as XXX", so that only those frames get dissected as XXX and other frames can be dissected as something else.

> they seem to indicate that the ID indicates the content of the message in some form, so it's more like an EtherType field than an address.

Technically the CAN ID is a priority for bus access control. In practice it is uses as a combination of bus access priority and identification of the payload.

> It depends on whether there will ever be a need for a user to say "dissect all CAN messages where no dissector is registered for a given ID and where no heuristic matches the contents as this protocol".

I think we won't get an answer to that. Personally I prefer Option A because it's a clean solution and because I have no use for the `Decode As` Feature. (At least at the moment)
But if I would be someone who is actually using `can.subdissector` I would be very disappointed if that dissector table gets removed. For this reason I would go with Option B.

I stumbled of the CAN sub dissectors a little while ago too and a cleanup might make a lot of sense!

Currently the usage of "dissect as" as well as the "heuristics dissection" seems to be a crutch to overcome that you cannot order the sub dissectors and some of them would just take all they get.


It is a bit complicated since depending on the sub dissector a different behavior is required/expected:
- AUTOSAR NM wants no error frames, no RTR frames, and filter with a value + mask:
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-autosar-nm.c#L392

- CANOPEN/DeviceNet/ISOBUS want no errors frames, no RTR frames, and only all standard IDs:
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-canopen.c#L1265
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-devicenet.c#L421
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-isobus.c#L320

- ISO15765 wants no error frames, no RTR frames, and works on everything it gets!? 
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-iso15765.c#L182

- J1939/UAVCAN want no error frames and only standard IDs but works on everything it gets (RTR too!?):
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-j1939.c#L173
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-uavcan-can.c#L178

- Signal PDU has a configuration of the IDs it wants:
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-signal-pdu.c#L1429

- OBD II has a hard coded CAN IDs in standard and extended, ERROR and RTR are not dissected:
  https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-obd-ii.c#L1359


So this is a quite heterogeneous set of requirements. I guess that the RTR for J1939 and UAVCAN might make not much sense, since RTR frames carry no data; hence, the sub dissector cannot do much with that. And the sub dissectors try to parse non existing bytes it seems on first glance. So this seems like a bug.

If that can be resolved, we could change AUTOSAR NM to generate all possible CAN IDs out of the Mask+Value combination. I would expect the entries generated in the CAN sub dissector would be in the hundreds or thousands. Probably good enough.

For the ISO15765 dissector, I assume changing to value+mask, values, or ranges could work too. You typically know on which CAN IDs the protocol runs.

And you would also need to update all protocols carrying CAN:
- packet-tecmp.c
- packet-socketcan.c
- packet-ieee1722.c
- packet-caneth.c


And one more thing... its not CAN alone. FlexRay has the same issue too. The good thing: This would only need to be changed in:
- packet-flexray.h
- packet-flexray.c
- packet-signal-pdu.c
- packet-tecmp.c

Changing FlexRay is rather easy. The ID is made up by a 16bit, a 8bit, and another 8bit value. While you could write the configs in a split fashion, you probably need to use a combined uint32 for the sub dissector table. Since you need to consider all combined.

P.S. Combination of sub dissectors is mainly for an automotive use case. Here you might want to use in parallel and based on CAN IDs: AUTOSAR NM, ISO15765, Signal PDU, and OBD II.

Thanks for the detailed description. Since changing `can.subdissector` would affect many other protocols I would propose to go with the following:

- Introduce two new (FT_UINT32) dissector tables `can.id` and `can.extended_id` which contain the pure CAN ID without any bit coding magic
- Also keep existing `can.subdissector` with its current implementation
- `can.id` and `can.extended_id` **get priority** over the existing `can.subdissector` as they are more specific. This means if `can.id` or`can.extended_id` would have a match `can.subdissector` would not be called.
- If someone does not use the new `can.id` and `can.extended_id` then `can.subdissector` would be called as it was before. (Heuristic dissectors would be called before `can.subdissector` if `heuristic_first` is set to true)

Other protocols have the possiblity to migrate to `can.id` and `can.extended_id` as they want. As I did understand for some of them this change would be very welcome as it would enable cleaner and simpler implementations on their side.

Do you agree to that?

Since updating this merge request exceeds my git skills I created a new merge request with an implementation according to my previous proposal:

[can: more specific dissector tables for CAN IDs and extended IDs](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/3405)

This makes sense, especially in view of the fact that the direction of the change has changed slightly.

The instructions for amending an MR can be found [here](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/wikis/Development/SubmittingPatches#amending-a-change), amending an MR is generally preferred as you keep all the relevant discussion on a single MR, rather than having to chase down cross links.

Anyway it's done now.
